title: Grape Identification Techniques
quiz.0.question: In blind tasting, which Italian red grape is known for being "pale with an orange-red rim, yet very high in acidity and powerful tannins"?
quiz.0.explanation: Nebbiolo's classic profile is a pale colour that easily shows an orange-red rim, yet very high acidity and powerful tannins on the palate — "a wolf in sheep's clothing": gentle to the eye but powerfully structured.
quiz.1.question: You smell clear "sour cherry" and "tomato leaf", and the tannins feel dusty. Which grape is it most likely to be?
quiz.1.explanation: Sour cherry (note: "sour", not sweet) with tomato leaf and dried herbs is Sangiovese's most classic aroma signature, and Tuscan soils give its tannins a dusty texture.
quiz.2.question: Aglianico is often called "the Barolo of the South". What is its biggest difference from Nebbiolo in blind tasting?
quiz.2.options.1: Aglianico is deep and opaque, with black fruit and volcanic-ash aromas
quiz.2.options.2: Aglianico has no tannin at all
quiz.2.explanation: Both have high acid and high tannin, but Aglianico is deep in colour (Nebbiolo is pale), and its aromas lean towards black fruit and smoky volcanic notes (Nebbiolo leans towards red fruit and flowers).
quiz.3.question: In Piemonte, which grape's blind-tasting profile is "high acidity but very low tannin", in sharp contrast to Nebbiolo?
quiz.3.explanation: Barbera's classic structure is high acidity with low tannin, which makes it easy to tell apart from high-tannin Nebbiolo in blind tasting.
slides.0.title: Grape Identification Techniques
slides.0.subtitle: Recognising the signature features of Italian red and white grapes
slides.1.title: The Core of Grape Identification in Italian Blind Tasting
slides.1.content:
Italy has 350+ native grapes, but in blind tasting you only need to master about 10 "highly recognisable" grapes to handle most exam questions and real-life situations. The key is finding each grape's "signature".

🔑 The signature principle

Each grape has 1-2 unique signatures

Finding the signature narrows the field dramatically. Use the other features to confirm, not to overturn

🔍 Thinking by elimination

"What this cannot be" is more useful than "what this is"

High acid + high tannin + pale → rule out Primitivo/Nero d'Avola → leaves Nebbiolo/Sangiovese → decide by aroma

⚠️ The most common Italian misjudgement

Nebbiolo mistaken for Pinot Noir

Both are pale, but Nebbiolo shows more orange, and on the palate very high acid + high tannin (Pinot Noir usually has medium-high acid and medium-low tannin)

📊 Training focus

Comparative tasting works best

Nebbiolo vs Sangiovese | Barbera vs Dolcetto | Aglianico vs Sagrantino
slides.2.title: Quick Reference: Red Grape Signatures
slides.2.content:
The signature features of Italy's six main red grapes side by side — master these to handle most blind-tasting situations.

Northern grapes

  • Nebbiolo: pale + orange rim | rose + tar | very high acid + very high tannin
  • Barbera: medium depth | red fruit + a little vanilla | high acid + low tannin (the exact opposite of Nebbiolo)
  • Dolcetto: deep purple (young) | black plum + liquorice | low acid + medium tannin (with a bitter finish)

Central and southern grapes

  • Sangiovese: medium garnet | sour cherry + tomato leaf + dried herbs | high acid + medium-high tannin
  • Aglianico: deep purple-black | black fruit + smoky volcanic notes | high acid + very high tannin (the South's strongest tannins)
  • Primitivo: deep purple-red | blackberry jam + chocolate + spice | low acid + medium tannin + high alcohol
slides.3.title: Nebbiolo vs Sangiovese: The Hardest Pair to Tell Apart
slides.3.content:
Both have high acidity and clear Italian native character — the pair most often confused in blind tasting.

Nebbiolo

  • Colour: pale garnet, high transparency, orange rim (even when young)
  • Signature aromas: 🌹 rose petal + 🛢️ tar (its most classic identifying combination)
  • Spice: liquorice, star anise, violet
  • Acidity: very high (pH 3.2-3.5)
  • Tannins: very high, fine as silk ("steel wrapped in silk")
  • Examples: Barolo DOCG, Barbaresco DOCG

Sangiovese

  • Colour: medium garnet, medium transparency, orange rim only after 5 years
  • Signature aromas: 🍒 sour cherry + 🌿 dried herbs
  • Spice: tomato leaf, rosemary, thyme
  • Acidity: high (pH 3.3-3.6)
  • Tannins: medium-high, with a dusty texture (not silky)
  • Examples: Brunello DOCG, Chianti Classico DOCG
slides.4.title: Signature Features of White Grapes
slides.4.content:
A shared trait of Italian whites in blind tasting: a bitter-almond finish is the most reliable Italian white signature

🥂 Garganega (Soave): chamomile + white peach + almond | round texture | a clear bitter-almond finish | medium acidity
🌿 Verdicchio (Marche): fennel + green apple + minerality | high acidity | strong ageing potential | the name comes from verde (green), and it often shows green glints
🍯 Fiano (Campania): honey + roasted hazelnut + a waxy texture | one of the South's most complex whites | more distinctive with age
🧊 Pinot Grigio (northern Italy): green apple + lemon + minerality | light and crisp | high acidity but fairly neutral fruit | the most "international" Italian white
slides.5.title: Key Takeaways
slides.5.points.0: Master 10 highly recognisable grapes to handle most Italian blind-tasting situations
slides.5.points.1: Nebbiolo signature: pale + orange rim + rose and tar + very high acid and very high tannin
slides.5.points.2: Sangiovese signature: medium garnet + sour cherry + dried herbs + medium-high dusty tannins
slides.5.points.3: Aglianico signature: deep purple-black + black fruit and smoky volcanic notes + high acid and very high tannin (the South's strongest)
slides.5.points.4: Barbera: high acid + low tannin, Piemonte's greatest contrast with Nebbiolo
slides.5.points.5: Primitivo: deep colour + blackberry jam and chocolate + low acid and high alcohol (a warm-climate southern grape)
slides.5.points.6: The shared signature of Italian whites: a bitter-almond finish, the key clue distinguishing them from whites of other countries
slides.5.points.7: Garganega signature: chamomile + white peach + bitter almond | Fiano signature: honey + roasted hazelnut
slides.5.points.8: The most common misjudgement: Nebbiolo ≠ Pinot Noir (very high acid and tannin on the palate rule out Pinot Noir at once)
slides.6.title: Grape Identification Knowledge Check
slides.6.questions.0.question: Which Italian red grape is known for being "pale with an orange-red rim, yet very high in acidity and powerful tannins"?
slides.6.questions.0.explanation: Nebbiolo is low in anthocyanins, pale with an orange-red rim, yet very high in acidity and powerful tannins on the palate — gentle to the eye but powerfully structured, the most iconic "contrast grape" of Italian blind tasting.
slides.6.questions.1.question: You smell "sour cherry + tomato leaf", and the tannins feel dusty. Which grape is it most likely to be?
slides.6.questions.1.explanation: Sour cherry (stress on "sour") with tomato leaf and dried herbs is Sangiovese's most classic aroma signature, and Tuscan soils give its tannins their characteristic dusty texture.
slides.6.questions.2.question: What is the biggest difference between Aglianico ("the Barolo of the South") and Nebbiolo in blind tasting?
slides.6.questions.2.options.1: Aglianico is deep and opaque, with black fruit and volcanic-ash aromas
slides.6.questions.2.options.2: Aglianico has no tannin at all
slides.6.questions.2.explanation: Both have high acid and high tannin, but Aglianico is deep in colour (Nebbiolo is pale), and its aromas lean towards black fruit and smoky volcanic notes (Nebbiolo leans towards red fruit and flowers).
slides.6.questions.3.question: In Piemonte, which grape has "high acidity but very low tannin", in sharp contrast to Nebbiolo?
slides.6.questions.3.explanation: Barbera's classic structure is high acidity with low tannin, which makes it easy to tell apart from high-tannin Nebbiolo in blind tasting — the exact opposite structure within the same region.
slides.6.questions.4.question: What finish characteristic is most commonly shared by Italian whites in blind tasting?
slides.6.questions.4.options.1: A slightly bitter almond note on the finish (bitter almond)
slides.6.questions.4.options.2: Very low acidity and a sweet palate
slides.6.questions.4.explanation: A bitter-almond finish is a classic trait shared by many Italian white grapes (Garganega, Verdicchio, Cortese) and an important clue for distinguishing Italian whites from those of other countries.
